guide.title: Interview Guide - European Electric Bus Adoption

questions.text: How would you describe current adoption of electric buses in your market?
What are the main barriers to adoption?
How important are budgets and total cost of ownership in purchasing decisions?
How important are driver training and vehicle reliability?
What adoption trend do you expect over the next 3-5 years?
What is the typical decision-making timeline for purchasing a new bus fleet?

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: Thanks for making time. How would you describe electric bus adoption in the Netherlands today?

segments.speaker: Sanne de Vries
segments.text: Adoption is well advanced compared with most of Europe, but it is concentrated in the larger city concessions where the depots have already been upgraded. Smaller regional operators are moving much more slowly.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What is holding the slower operators back?

segments.speaker: Sanne de Vries
segments.text: Depot charging capacity is the biggest issue. The buses themselves are available, but a grid connection upgrade can take longer than the vehicle order itself.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: So is the decision mainly financial?

segments.speaker: Sanne de Vries
segments.text: Total cost of ownership decides it. The purchase price is higher, so the case has to be made on energy and maintenance savings over the concession period, and the finance team will not approve without that.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What about driver training?

segments.speaker: Sanne de Vries
segments.text: Training matters more than people expect in the first year. Drivers change their braking and route behaviour, and if only part of the depot is trained the range figures we promised do not hold.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: And reliability?

segments.speaker: Sanne de Vries
segments.text: Reliability is good now, but availability during winter is still the number people ask about, because heating draws from the same battery.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What do you expect over the next three to five years?

segments.speaker: Sanne de Vries
segments.text: I expect continued growth, steadily rather than sharply. In the larger city fleets I would expect something like 20 to 25 percent more electric vehicles each year, while the smaller operators stay well behind that.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: How long does a fleet purchase normally take?

segments.speaker: Sanne de Vries
segments.text: Six to twelve months once the operator is serious, though it stretches if the depot upgrade has to go through a separate approval.

transcripts.role: Former Procurement Director, Municipal Transport Authority

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: How would you describe electric bus adoption in Poland today?

segments.speaker: Marek Kowalski
segments.text: It is growing but very uneven. A few large cities have committed fully, while many mid-sized municipalities are still running pilot routes.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What are the main barriers?

segments.speaker: Marek Kowalski
segments.text: Purchase price is the first barrier. These are large capital items and municipal budgets are tight. The second issue is proving the buses will be used enough to justify the cost.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What does procurement actually look at?

segments.speaker: Marek Kowalski
segments.text: We look at total cost of ownership, expected daily kilometres, battery warranty, service contracts and training requirements. Environmental commitments help, but the financial case decides whether it gets approved.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: How important is driver training?

segments.speaker: Marek Kowalski
segments.text: Very important operationally. If the depot buys vehicles but only a few drivers are comfortable with them, utilisation drops and the business case weakens.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: Do you expect adoption to accelerate?

segments.speaker: Marek Kowalski
segments.text: Yes, but I would not expect a dramatic jump. Growth will be gradual, because cities have competing capital priorities such as track renewal.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: Any rough expectation for the next three to five years?

segments.speaker: Marek Kowalski
segments.text: I would expect continued growth, but closer to high single digits or low double digits across the whole national fleet, rather than anything like 25 percent.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: How long can the purchase process take?

segments.speaker: Marek Kowalski
segments.text: Twelve to eighteen months is common. Procurement, the operator, finance and the city council all have to align, so it moves slowly.

transcripts.role: Head of Sustainable Mobility, City Transit Agency

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: How would you describe adoption in Spain?

segments.speaker: Elena Navarro
segments.text: Adoption is increasing, and in some larger city agencies electric buses are becoming the default for new orders. Access still varies a lot between cities.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What are the main barriers?

segments.speaker: Elena Navarro
segments.text: Funding matters, but I would say depot and workshop readiness is just as important. You can order vehicles, but if the depot cannot charge and service them the rollout stalls.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: How important is total cost of ownership?

segments.speaker: Elena Navarro
segments.text: It matters, but the discussion is not purely financial. Agencies also weigh air quality commitments, passenger experience and whether the fleet helps them win the next concession.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: So would you say economics are less important in Spain?

segments.speaker: Elena Navarro
segments.text: I would say economics and policy commitments are balanced. I would not say the financial case alone decides the purchase.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What is your outlook for the next three to five years?

segments.speaker: Elena Navarro
segments.text: I am quite positive. Adoption could accelerate if depot funding expands and vehicle prices keep falling. I could see fleet growth above 15 percent annually in some regions.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: What about purchase timelines?

segments.speaker: Elena Navarro
segments.text: Around six to nine months can happen when the funding is already allocated. If the agency has to wait for a new budget cycle it takes considerably longer.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: Any final thought?

segments.speaker: Elena Navarro
segments.text: The main point is that adoption is not just about buying vehicles. Agencies need trained drivers, ready depots and enough daily kilometres for the programme to hold together.

hot_questions.question: Does the financial case decide purchases?
hot_questions.why_flagged: This is the core approval question, with two speakers saying finance decides and one explicitly qualifying that view.
hot_questions.answer: Sanne de Vries said total cost of ownership is decisive, with approval dependent on making the case from energy and maintenance savings. Marek Kowalski similarly said environmental commitments help, but the financial case determines approval. Elena Navarro pushed back on a finance-only view, saying the discussion is not purely financial and that economics and policy commitments are balanced.

hot_questions.question: Are depots the main rollout bottleneck?
hot_questions.why_flagged: Depot readiness is a repeated operational risk that can stall deployment even when vehicles or funding are available.
hot_questions.answer: Sanne de Vries identified depot charging capacity as the biggest issue and said grid upgrades can take longer than vehicle orders. Elena Navarro said depot and workshop readiness is as important as funding, because rollout stalls if depots cannot charge and service buses. Sanne also qualified purchase timing by noting that separate depot-upgrade approval can stretch the process.

agreements.nuance: The markets are at different maturity levels: the Netherlands is described as relatively advanced, Poland as still uneven with pilots in many mid-sized municipalities, and Spain as increasing with some large agencies making electric buses the default for new orders.
